Main.sentence: James Earl Carter Jr. (October 1, 1924 – December 29, 2024) was an American politician and humanitarian who served as the 39th ___E:president of the United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States)___ from 1977 to 1981. A member of the ___E:Democratic Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States))___ , Carter served from 1971 to 1975 as the 76th ___E:governor of Georgia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Georgia)___ and from 1963 to 1967 in the ___E:Georgia State Senate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_State_Senate)___ .

He was the ___E:longest-lived president in U.S. history U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_age)___ and the only one to reach the ___E:age of 100 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_100)___ .

Born in ___E:Plains, Georgia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plains,_Georgia)___ , Carter graduated from the ___E:U.S. Naval Academy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Naval_Academy)___ in 1946 and joined the ___E:submarine service U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submarines_in_the_United_States_Navy)___ before returning to his family's peanut farm. He was active in the ___E:civil rights movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights_movement)___ , then served as a ___E:state senator U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_senator)___ and the ___E:76th governor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_governors_of_Georgia)___ , one of the first of the " ___E:New South governors U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_South_governor)___ " committed to ___E:desegregation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desegregation_in_the_United_States)___ .

After announcing ___E:his candidacy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter_1976_presidential_campaign)___ in ___E:1976 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_United_States_presidential_election)___ , Carter secured the ___E:Democratic nomination U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_Democratic_National_Convention)___ as a ___E:dark horse U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_horse)___ little known outside his home state before narrowly defeating ___E:Republican U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States))___ incumbent ___E:Gerald Ford U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Ford)___ in the general election.

As president, Carter ___E:pardoned all Vietnam draft evaders U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proclamation_4483)___ and negotiated major foreign policy agreements, including the ___E:Camp David Accords U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camp_David_Accords)___ , the ___E:Panama Canal Treaties U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama_Canal_Treaties)___ , and the second round of ___E:Strategic Arms Limitation Talks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_Arms_Limitation_Talks)___ , and he ___E:established diplomatic relations with China U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Communiqu%C3%A9_on_the_Establishment_of_Diplomatic_Relations)___ .
He created a national energy policy that included conservation, price control, and new technology.

He signed bills that created the Departments ___E:of Energy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Energy)___ and ___E:Education U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education)___ .

The later years of ___E:his presidency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Jimmy_Carter)___ were marked by several foreign policy crises, including the ___E:Soviet invasion of Afghanistan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_invasion_of_Afghanistan)___ (leading to the end of détente and the ___E:1980 Olympics boycott U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Olympics_boycott)___ ) and the fallout of the ___E:Iranian Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_Revolution)___ (including the ___E:Iran hostage crisis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran_hostage_crisis)___ and ___E:1979 oil crisis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1979_oil_crisis)___ ).

Carter ___E:sought reelection U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter_1980_presidential_campaign)___ in ___E:1980 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_United_States_presidential_election)___ , defeating ___E:a primary challenge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries)___ by Senator ___E:Ted Kennedy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Kennedy)___ , but lost the election to Republican nominee ___E:Ronald Reagan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan)___ .

Polls of historians and political scientists have ___E:ranked Carter's presidency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_rankings_of_presidents_of_the_United_States)___ below average. ___E:His post-presidency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-presidency_of_Jimmy_Carter)___ —the longest in U.S. history—is viewed more favorably.

After Carter's presidential term ended, he established the ___E:Carter Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carter_Center)___ to promote human rights, earning him the 2002 ___E:Nobel Peace Prize U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize)___ .

He traveled extensively to conduct peace negotiations, ___E:monitor elections U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Election_monitoring)___ , and end ___E:neglected tropical diseases U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neglected_tropical_diseases)___ , becoming a major contributor to the ___E:eradication of dracunculiasis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eradication_of_dracunculiasis)___ .
Carter was a key figure in the nonprofit housing organization ___E:Habitat for Humanity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habitat_for_Humanity)___ .

He also ___E:wrote political memoirs and other books U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bibliography_of_Jimmy_Carter#Books_by_Carter)___ , commentary on the ___E:Israeli–Palestinian conflict U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_conflict)___ , and poetry.

James Earl Carter Jr. was born on October 1, 1924, in ___E:Plains, Georgia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plains,_Georgia)___ , at the ___E:Wise Sanitarium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wise_Sanitarium)___ , where his mother worked as a registered nurse.
Carter was the first U.S. president born in a hospital.

He was the eldest child of ___E:Bessie Lillian Gordy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessie_Lillian_Gordy)___ and ___E:James Earl Carter Sr. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Earl_Carter_Sr.)___ , and a descendant of English immigrant Thomas Carter, who settled in the ___E:Colony of Virginia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colony_of_Virginia)___ in 1635.   In Georgia, numerous generations of Carters worked as cotton farmers.

Carter's father was a successful local businessman who ran a ___E:general store U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_store)___ and was an investor in farmland;  he had served as a reserve second lieutenant in the ___E:U.S. Army Quartermaster Corps U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Army_Quartermaster_Corps)___ during ___E:World War I U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I)___ .

During Carter's infancy, his family moved several times, settling on a dirt road in nearby ___E:Archery U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery,_Georgia)___ , which was almost entirely populated by impoverished Black families.

His family eventually had three more children, ___E:Gloria U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloria_Carter_Spann)___ , ___E:Ruth U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Carter_Stapleton)___ , and ___E:Billy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Carter)___ .
Carter had a good relationship with his parents, even though his mother was often absent during his childhood since she worked long hours.
Although his father was staunchly ___E:pro-segregation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_segregation_in_the_United_States)___ , he allowed Jimmy to befriend the Black farmhands' children.
Carter was an enterprising teenager who was given his own acre of Earl's farmland, where he grew and sold peanuts.
Carter also rented out a section of tenant housing he had purchased.
Carter attended Plains High School from 1937 to 1941, graduating from the 11th grade; the school did not have a 12th grade.

By that time, Archery and Plains had been impoverished by the ___E:Great Depression U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression_in_the_United_States)___ , but the family benefited from ___E:New Deal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Deal)___ farming subsidies, and Carter's father became a community leader.
Carter was a diligent student with a fondness for reading.

According to a popular anecdote, he was passed over for ___E:valedictorian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valedictorian)___ after he and his friends skipped school to venture downtown in a ___E:hot rod U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_rod)___ (although it is not clear he would otherwise have been valedictorian).

Carter played on the Plains High School basketball team and joined ___E:Future Farmers of America U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Future_Farmers_of_America)___ , which helped him develop a lifelong interest in woodworking.
Carter had long dreamed of attending the ___E:United States Naval Academy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Naval_Academy)___ .
In 1941, he started undergraduate coursework in engineering at ___E:Georgia Southwestern College U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Southwestern_College)___ in nearby Americus, Georgia.
The next year, Carter transferred to the ___E:Georgia School of Technology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_School_of_Technology)___ (now Georgia Tech) in Atlanta.
While at Georgia Tech, Carter took part in the ___E:Reserve Officers' Training Corps U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reserve_Officers%27_Training_Corps)___ .
Civil rights icon ___E:Blake Van Leer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blake_Van_Leer)___ encouraged Carter to join the Naval Academy.
In 1943, he received an appointment to the Naval Academy from U.S.

Representative ___E:Stephen Pace U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Pace_(politician))___ , and Carter graduated with a Bachelor of Science in 1946.   He was a good student, but was seen as reserved and quiet, in contrast to the academy's culture of aggressive hazing of freshmen.

While at the academy, Carter fell in love with ___E:Rosalynn Smith U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosalynn_Smith)___ , a friend of his sister Ruth.  The two wed shortly after his graduation in 1946, and were married until her death on November 19, 2023.   Carter was a ___E:sprint football U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sprint_football)___ player for the ___E:Navy Midshipmen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navy_Midshipmen)___ and a standout freshman ___E:cross country runner U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navy_Midshipmen_cross_country)___ .
He graduated 60th out of 821 midshipmen in the class of 1947 [a] with a Bachelor of Science degree and was commissioned as an ___E:ensign U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ensign_(rank))___ .

From 1946 to 1953, the Carters lived in ___E:Virginia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia)___ , ___E:Hawaii U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territory_of_Hawaii)___ , ___E:Connecticut U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connecticut)___ , ___E:New York U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state))___ , and ___E:California U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California)___ , during his deployments in ___E:the Atlantic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Atlantic_Fleet)___ and ___E:Pacific fleets U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Pacific_Fleet)___ .
In 1948, he began officer training for submarine duty and served aboard ___E:USS Pomfret U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Pomfret)___ .

Carter was promoted to ___E:lieutenant junior grade U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant_junior_grade)___ in 1949. His service aboard Pomfret included a simulated war patrol to the western Pacific and Chinese coast from January to March of that year.  In 1951, Carter was assigned to the diesel/electric ___E:USS K-1 (SSK-1) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Barracuda_(SSK-1))___ , qualified for command, and served in several positions, including executive officer.

In 1952, Carter began an association with the Navy's fledgling ___E:nuclear submarine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_submarine)___ program, led by then-Captain ___E:Hyman G. Rickover U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyman_G._Rickover)___ .

Rickover had high standards, and Carter later said that, next to his parents, Rickover had the greatest influence on his life.  Carter was sent to the ___E:Naval Reactors U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Reactors)___ Branch of the ___E:Atomic Energy Commission U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Atomic_Energy_Commission)___ in Washington, D.C., for three-month temporary duty, while Rosalynn moved with their children to ___E:Schenectady, New York U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schenectady,_New_York)___ .

On December 12, 1952, an accident with the experimental ___E:NRX U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRX)___ reactor at ___E:Atomic Energy of Canada U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_Energy_of_Canada)___ 's ___E:Chalk River Laboratories U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chalk_River_Laboratories)___ caused a partial ___E:meltdown U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_meltdown)___ .
Carter was ordered to Chalk River to lead a U.S. maintenance crew to assist in the shutdown of the reactor.

The painstaking process required each team member to don protective gear and be lowered individually into the reactor for 90 seconds at a time, limiting their exposure to radioactivity while they disassembled the crippled reactor.

During and after his presidency, Carter said that his experience at Chalk River had shaped his views on atomic energy and led him to cease the development of a ___E:neutron bomb U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_bomb)___ .
In March 1953, Carter began a six-month nuclear power plant operation course at ___E:Union College U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_College)___ in Schenectady.
His intent was to eventually work aboard ___E:USS Seawolf U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Seawolf_(SSN-575))___ , which was intended to be the second U.S. nuclear submarine.

His plans changed when his father died of ___E:pancreatic cancer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pancreatic_cancer)___ in July, two months before construction of Seawolf began, and Carter obtained a release from active duty so he could take over the family peanut business.
Deciding to leave Schenectady proved difficult, as Rosalynn had grown comfortable with their life there.
She later said that returning to small-town life in Plains seemed "a monumental step backward".

Carter left active duty on October 9, 1953.   He served in the inactive ___E:Navy Reserve U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy_Reserve)___ until 1961 and left with the rank of ___E:lieutenant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant_(navy))___ .

Carter's awards include the ___E:American Campaign Medal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Campaign_Medal)___ , ___E:World War II Victory Medal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II_Victory_Medal)___ , ___E:China Service Medal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Service_Medal)___ , and ___E:National Defense Service Medal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Defense_Service_Medal)___ .
As a submarine officer, he also earned the ___E:"dolphin" badge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submarine_Warfare_insignia)___ .
After debt settlements and division of his father's estate, Jimmy inherited comparatively little.
For a year, he, Rosalynn, and their three sons lived in public housing in Plains. [b] Carter set out to expand the family's peanut-growing business.
Transitioning from the Navy to farming was difficult as his first-year harvest failed due to drought, and Carter had to open several lines of credit to keep the farm afloat.
He took classes and studied agriculture while Rosalynn learned accounting to manage the business's books.
Though they barely broke even the first year, the Carters grew the business and became quite successful.

As racial tension inflamed in Plains by the 1954 ___E:Supreme Court of the United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States)___ ruling in Brown v. Board of Education ,  Carter favored integration but often kept those feelings to himself to avoid making enemies.

By 1961, Carter began to speak more prominently of integration as a member of the ___E:Baptist Church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptist_Church)___ and chairman of the ___E:Sumter County U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sumter_County,_Georgia)___ school board.

In 1962, he announced his campaign for an open ___E:Georgia State Senate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_State_Senate)___ seat.  Rosalynn, who had an instinct for politics and organization, was instrumental in his campaign.
While early counting of the ballots showed Carter trailing his opponent, Homer Moore, this was later proven to be the result of fraudulent voting.
Another election was held, in which Carter defeated Moore as the sole Democratic candidate.

He served in both the ___E:127th Georgia General Assembly U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/127th_Georgia_General_Assembly)___ and the ___E:128th Georgia General Assembly U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/128th_Georgia_General_Assembly)___ .
The ___E:civil rights movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights_movement)___ was well underway when Carter took office.
Carter remained relatively quiet on the issue at first, even as it polarized much of the county, to avoid alienating his segregationist colleagues.

Carter did speak up on a few divisive issues, giving speeches against ___E:literacy tests U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literacy_test)___ and against an amendment to the ___E:Georgia Constitution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Georgia_(U.S._state))___ that he felt implied a compulsion to practice religion.
Carter entered the state Democratic Executive Committee two years into office, where he helped rewrite the state party's rules.
He became the chairman of the West Central Georgia Planning and Development Commission, which oversaw the disbursement of federal and state grants for projects such as historic site restoration.

When ___E:Bo Callaway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bo_Callaway)___ was elected to the ___E:United States House of Representatives U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives)___ in 1964, Carter immediately began planning to challenge him. The two had previously clashed over which two-year college would be expanded to a four-year college program by the state, and Carter saw Callaway—who had switched to the ___E:Republican Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States))___ —as representing aspects of politics he despised.
Carter was reelected to a second two-year term in the state Senate,  where he chaired its Education Committee and sat on the Appropriations Committee.

He contributed to a bill expanding statewide education funding and getting ___E:Georgia Southwestern State University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Southwestern_State_University)___ a four-year program.
He leveraged his regional planning work, giving speeches around the district to make himself more visible to potential voters.
On the last day of the term, Carter announced his candidacy for the House of Representatives.
Callaway decided to run for governor instead;  Carter decided to do the same.

In the 1966 gubernatorial election, Carter ran against liberal former governor ___E:Ellis Arnall U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellis_Arnall)___ and conservative segregationist ___E:Lester Maddox U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Maddox)___ in the Democratic primary.
In a press conference, he described his ideology as "Conservative, moderate, liberal and middle-of-the-road ...

I believe I am a more complicated person than that."  He lost the primary but drew enough votes as a third-place candidate to force Arnall into a ___E:runoff election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runoff_election)___ with Maddox, who defeated Arnall.

In the general election, Republican nominee Callaway won a plurality of the vote but less than a majority, allowing the Democratic-majority ___E:Georgia House of Representatives U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_House_of_Representatives)___ to elect Maddox as governor.
Maddox's victory—due to his segregationist stance—was seen as the worst outcome for the indebted Carter.
Carter returned to his agriculture business, carefully planning his next campaign.
This period was a spiritual turning point for Carter; he declared himself a ___E:born again U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Born_again)___ Christian.
His last child, ___E:Amy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amy_Carter)___ , was born during this time.
In the 1970 gubernatorial election, liberal former governor ___E:Carl Sanders U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders)___ became Carter's main opponent in the Democratic primary.
Carter ran a more modern campaign, employing printed graphics and statistical analysis.

Responding to polls, he leaned more conservative than before, positioning himself as a ___E:populist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Populist)___ and criticizing Sanders for both his wealth and perceived links to the national Democratic Party.
He also accused Sanders of corruption, but when pressed by the media, he did not provide evidence.

Throughout his campaign, Carter sought both the black vote and the votes of those who had supported prominent Alabama segregationist ___E:George Wallace U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Wallace)___ .

While he met with black figures such as ___E:Martin Luther King Sr. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Sr.)___ and ___E:Andrew Young U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Young)___ and visited many black-owned businesses, he also praised Wallace and promised to invite him to give a speech in Georgia.
Carter's appeal to racism became more blatant over time, with his senior campaign aides handing out a photograph of Sanders celebrating with Black basketball players.
Carter came ahead of Sanders in the first ballot, leading to a runoff election.
The subsequent campaign was even more bitter.

Despite his early support for civil rights, Carter's appeal to racism grew, and he criticized Sanders for supporting ___E:Martin Luther King Jr. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr.)___ Carter won the runoff election and won the general election against Republican nominee ___E:Hal Suit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hal_Suit)___ .

Once elected, Carter began to speak against Georgia's racist politics. ___E:Leroy Johnson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leroy_Johnson_(Georgia_politician))___ , a black state senator, voiced his support for Carter: "I understand why he ran that kind of ultra-conservative campaign.
I don't believe you can win this state without being a racist."

Carter was sworn in as the 76th ___E:governor of Georgia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Georgia)___ on January 12, 1971. In his inaugural speech, he declared that "the time for racial discrimination is over",  shocking the crowd and causing many segregationists who had supported his candidacy to feel betrayed.
Carter was reluctant to engage with fellow politicians, making him unpopular with the legislature.

He expanded the governor's authority by introducing a reorganization plan submitted in January 1972. Despite an initially cool reception in the legislature, the plan passed at midnight on the last day of the session.
Carter merged about 300 state agencies into 22, although it is disputed whether that saved the state money.
On July 8, 1971, during an appearance in ___E:Columbus, Georgia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus,_Georgia)___ , he stated his intention to establish a Georgia Human Rights Council.

In a July 1971 news conference, Carter announced that he had ordered department heads to reduce spending to prevent a $57 million deficit by the end of the 1972 fiscal year, specifying that each state department would be affected and estimating that five percent over government revenue would be lost if state departments continued to fully use allocated funds.

In January 1972, he requested that the state legislature fund an early childhood development program along with prison reform programs and $48 million (equivalent to $270 million in 2024) in paid taxes for nearly all state employees.
In March 1972, Carter said he might call a special session of the general assembly if the Justice Department struck down any reapportionment plans by either the House or Senate.
He pushed several reforms through the legislature, providing equal state aid to schools, setting up community centers for mentally disabled children, and increasing educational programs for convicts.

In one of his more controversial decisions, he vetoed a plan to build a dam on Georgia's ___E:Flint River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flint_River)___ , which attracted the attention of environmentalists nationwide.
Civil rights were a high priority for Carter, who added black state employees and portraits of three prominent black Georgians to the capitol building.
This angered the ___E:Ku Klux Klan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ku_Klux_Klan)___ .

He favored a constitutional amendment to ban ___E:busing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Busing)___ for the purpose of expediting integration in schools on a televised joint appearance with Florida Governor ___E:Reubin Askew U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reubin_Askew)___ on January 31, 1973,  and co-sponsored an anti-busing resolution with Wallace at the 1971 National Governors Conference.
After the U.S.

Supreme Court struck down Georgia's ___E:death penalty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment_in_Georgia_(U.S._state))___ statute in Furman v. Georgia (1972), Carter signed a revised statute that reintroduced the practice.

The following year, buildings connected to Carter's life were granted status as ___E:National Historic Sites U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Site_(United_States))___  and in 2021 were collectively renamed the ___E:Jimmy Carter National Historic Park U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter_National_Historic_Park)___ .

In 1991, Carter was made an honorary member of ___E:Phi Beta Kappa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phi_Beta_Kappa)___ at ___E:Kansas State University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_State_University)___ ,  and was elected to the ___E:American Philosophical Society U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Philosophical_Society)___ .
In 1998, the U.S.
Navy named the third and final ___E:Seawolf-class U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seawolf-class_submarine)___ submarine ___E:USS Jimmy Carter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Jimmy_Carter)___ .

Carter received the ___E:United Nations Prize in the Field of Human Rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Prize_in_the_Field_of_Human_Rights)___ , given in honor of human rights achievements,  and the ___E:Hoover Medal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoover_Medal)___ , recognizing engineers who have contributed to global causes.

Carter's 2002 ___E:Nobel Peace Prize U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize)___  was partially a response to president George W. Bush's threats of war against Iraq and Carter's criticism of the Bush administration.

In 2009, the ___E:Souther Field U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Souther_Field)___ Airport in ___E:Americus, Georgia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americus,_Georgia)___ , was renamed ___E:Jimmy Carter Regional Airport U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter_Regional_Airport)___ .

In November 2024, Carter received his 10th nomination for the ___E:Grammy Award for Best Spoken Word Album U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Spoken_Word_Album)___ for audio recordings of his books.

He won four times—for Our Endangered Values: America's Moral Crisis (2007), A Full Life: Reflections at 90 (2015), Faith: A Journey For All (2018), and Last Sunday in Plains: A Centennial Celebration (2024). [f] He is the most nominated and awarded recipient in the category.

On February 21, 2024, the ___E:White House Historical Association U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House_Historical_Association)___ unveiled its official 2024 White House Christmas ornament honoring Carter's naval service and efforts for peace.
